questions.question: What is UniSent and what makes it notable?
questions.ground_truth: UniSent is a universal sentiment lexicon covering over 1000 languages (including many low-resource ones), created from an English sentiment lexicon and a massively parallel Bible corpus. It is, to the authors' knowledge, the largest sentiment resource to date in terms of number of covered languages, and its quality is close to manually created resources.
expected_passages: In this paper, we introduce UniSent a universal sentiment lexica for 1000 languages created using an English sentiment lexicon and a massively parallel corpus in the Bible domain. To the best of our knowledge, UniSent is the largest sentiment resource to date in terms of number of covered languages, including many low resource languages.
We create and release Unisent, the first massively cross-lingual sentiment lexicon in more than 1000 languages.

questions.question: How does the Adapted Sentiment Pivot method create a lexicon for a new language?
questions.ground_truth: It projects an English sentiment lexicon across languages using a massively parallel corpus (annotation projection), then expands the vocabulary and applies unsupervised domain adaptation using embedding spaces - for example projecting via the Bible corpus and adapting to the Wikipedia domain by modelling the vocabulary shift between the two.
expected_passages: Our method is inspired by with a novel combination of vocabulary expansion and domain adaptation using embedding spaces.
In the adaptation step, we compute the shift between the vocabularies in the Bible and Wikipedia corpora.

questions.question: How is UniSent evaluated?
questions.ground_truth: It is evaluated against manually created gold-standard sentiment lexica in Czech, German, French, Macedonian and Spanish (general domain), and against an emoticon dataset for the Twitter domain, by splitting the data into a UniSent-Lexicon, a Baseline-Lexicon and a held-out Evaluation-Lexicon.
expected_passages: As the gold standard sentiment lexica, we chose manually created lexicon in Czech, German, French, Macedonian, and Spanish. These lexica contain general domain words (as opposed to Twitter or Bible). As gold standard for twitter domain we use emoticon dataset and perform emoticon sentiment prediction,.
To show that our adaptation method also works well on domains like Twitter, we propose a second evaluation in which we use Adapted Sentiment Pivot to predict the sentiment of emoticons in Twitter.

questions.question: What are the main results of the evaluation?
questions.ground_truth: UniSent clearly outperforms the baseline for all languages and its quality is close to manually annotated data. The domain-adaptation method brings only small improvements - for morphologically poor languages in the general domain, and for French and Spanish in the Twitter domain.
expected_passages: The results show that (i) UniSent clearly outperforms the baseline for all languages (ii) the quality of UniSent is close to manually annotated data (iii) the domain adaptation method brings small improvements for morphologically poor languages.
The results show that (i) UniSent clearly outperforms the baseline and (ii) our domain adaptation technique brings small improvements for French and Spanish.
